books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: John C. Calhoun, speech in the Senate, February 6, 1837

stimulus.source_note: John C. Calhoun, speech in the Senate, February 6, 1837. Public domain.
stimulus.text: I hold that in the present state of civilization, where two races of different origin, and distinguished by color, and other physical differences, as well as intellectual, are brought together, the relation now existing in the slaveholding States between the two, is, instead of an evil, a good—a positive good.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Calhoun’s argument rests most directly on the claim that

options.text: enslaved people had asked to remain enslaved.
options.misconception: Calhoun never claims consent; his argument rests on race and civilization, not on what enslaved people wanted.

options.text: the Constitution banned slavery in the territories.
options.misconception: Background from the books: Calhoun argued the opposite, that the Constitution protected slavery in the territories; a ban is what his opponents wanted.

options.text: racial differences made slavery the fitting Southern relation.
Northern factories depended on enslaved labor.
options.misconception: Background from the books: Northern mills bought Southern cotton, but Calhoun’s case here turns on race, not on factory demand.

rationales.A: Calhoun never claims consent; his argument rests on race and civilization, not on what enslaved people wanted.
rationales.B: Background from the books: Calhoun argued the opposite, that the Constitution protected slavery in the territories; a ban is what his opponents wanted.
rationales.C: Calhoun builds his “positive good” on difference itself: two races “distinguished by color” and intellect, brought together, need the relation slavery provides.
rationales.D: Background from the books: Northern mills bought Southern cotton, but Calhoun’s case here turns on race, not on factory demand.
rationales.general:
1. Follow his reasoning: he starts with races “of different origin” and “distinguished by color.”
2. See where that starting point leads: difference becomes the reason slavery fits.
3. Check the other options: consent, the Constitution, and factories never appear in his sentence, so none of them can carry his argument.
Remember: find the claim an argument starts from; the conclusion usually follows from it.
